findings.title: The knowledge check tests whether the child can repeat its own pack, not whether the pack is right
findings.target: Section 4 step 4 (probe.json), section 5 step 2, amendment 1 items 2-3, row 13
findings.argument: probe.json is 'twelve questions with answer keys and card ids' (lines 50-51), written by the pack's author. Under the original split (builder, then a fresh expert) the check at least tested transfer from the pack to a fresh window. Amendment 1 removes the split: one child writes the cards, pack.md and must-read.md (lines 134-136), then 'passes the knowledge check' in the same session with the pack still in its context (lines 137-139). Read literally, the questions, the answer keys and the answers all come from one session, and they are graded against keys that point at its own cards. A child whose pack is wrong, lopsided or missing the key mechanism scores 12 of 12, because the keys carry the same errors. The check cannot see what the pack leaves out, so it cannot tell an expert from a confident summariser. Row 13 (line 176) counts this check as one of three defences against a weak expert. The 10-of-12 threshold (line 61) has no basis: nothing calibrates it. In the owner's terms, the gate that should certify 'expert first' certifies only self-consistency.
findings.smallest_fix: Have the probe written blind, before the child starts. The field's Opus checker writes it from the question list (line 36) and from sources it opens itself, including at least four questions whose answers are not in any card the child returns. It grades against the sources, not the cards. Missed coverage questions go back to stage A as gaps. Remove 'probe.json' from the pack's outputs (line 51).

findings.title: Amendment 1 breaks the one property that delivered 'filled precisely, nothing unnecessary', and leaves it untestable
findings.target: Amendment 1 items 1-3 and 5 against section 1 and section 5 step 1; row 1
findings.argument: Section 1 (lines 10-11) and section 5 step 1 (lines 58-59) gave the requirement a testable form: a fresh session that reads the frozen pack and the must-read sources, 'no other file', so 'its context then holds the field and nothing else'. Amendment 1 has the researcher review in its own window (lines 137-139). That window also holds the research process: the question drafting, every card a reader returned (dropped ones included), the passages, the papers it opened and rejected, the tool chatter, and its own 60-90k-token pack written out as output. The checker runs after the child has absorbed the cards (lines 134-136), so a card dropped for a wrong number (line 46) leaves pack.md but not the child's head. Row 1's guarantee (line 159) therefore holds for the files but not for the reviewer. No gate looks at the window: gate A checks the pack's size and coverage (lines 52-54), not what the reviewing session read. So 'precisely' is now a wish. The fresh-session path already exists in the protocol, as an exception (lines 142-143).
findings.smallest_fix: Make line 142-143 the rule, not the exception. The child researches and freezes its pack, and the review is always done by a fresh session from the frozen pack hash plus must-read. That session's input manifest (pack hash, must-read list, the fixed list of our files) is checked by the schema script against its read calls. This is a mechanism a script can run, and it is the testable meaning of 'filled precisely'. It reverses part of amendment 1, so it needs the owner's word under rule 8 (line 104). Keep the owner's point that the same field line both researches and reviews.

findings.title: Nobody challenges a wrongly dismissed lead or a dropped field, which is the mistake that started this programme
findings.target: Section 6 refuter, row 2, section 5 step 4 verdicts, rule 3
findings.argument: The programme exists because one null result struck a family off the list (direction lines 4-7: 'instead of striking graphs ... off the list'; line 43: 'Not found is not does not work'). Yet the only adversary is aimed at 'the three strongest leads' (line 84, repeated in row 2, line 160). A verdict of 'wrong form' or 'wrong problem' (line 68), a lead the synthesis leaves out, and a whole field 'dropped with a note' after failing a gate (lines 94-95) are never attacked by anyone. Strong leads also go on to an experiment, which tests them anyway. Dismissals get no test at all, so a false negative is permanent. No row in amendment 2 names false negatives.
findings.smallest_fix: Retarget the one refuter instead of adding one: it attacks every 'wrong form' or 'wrong problem' verdict on a family, plus every field dropped at a gate, with the packs in hand. Leave the strongest leads to the owner's experiment table. Add one row: 'false negative: a family dismissed on thin evidence' -> refuter on dismissals.

findings.title: Which sources get in is decided by a search engine and Sonnet screens; the checker confirms transcription, not selection
findings.target: Section 4 steps 1-3, gate A, row 1, amendment 1 item 1
findings.argument: Readers 'find and read sources' (line 39) with one search tool, so the pack inherits the tool's ranking: popular papers, vendor blogs and well-marketed products come first. Negative and unpublished results rarely appear, and work outside 2023-2026 (line 37) never does. The checker 'confirms the number and its conditions' (lines 44-45): a vendor's claim copied faithfully passes, and so does an outlier picked over a replication that contradicts it. Gate A's coverage test (line 53) checks that questions are answered, not that the answers rest on a fair sample. Amendment 1 item 1 (lines 131-133) puts the screening, the very step that decides what the expert is, in helpers' hands. The child reads 'the best primary sources' in the original, but it picks them from helper-written cards, so its expertise sits on Sonnet's framing of each paper (its 'limits' and 'how strong' fields). The direction asks for vendor claims to be separated (direction line 68) and the earlier research to be read first (line 70), but the protocol has no rule that applies either. What is never seen is never named.
findings.smallest_fix: Two changes to existing steps. (a) The card's evidence field becomes an enum (replicated / independent / single-study / vendor's own), and the schema script marks any review verdict that rests only on vendor or single-study cards as 'judgment'. (b) Gate A's coverage check is run against a seed list the reader did not choose: the earlier research files (direction line 70) and the citations of the must-read papers. The pack states which seeds it omits and why. Also log every search query in the ledger, so the refuter can see what was never searched.

findings.title: A second expert of the same model, with the same search tool and the same question list, is not independent, and the comparison rule was written for a different design
findings.target: Section 6 first bullet, amendment 1 item 4, row 3
findings.argument: Line 77 says the second expert works 'from the same pack', and lines 79-80 read disagreement between 'two instances with the same knowledge' as a sign of a weak claim. Amendment 1 item 4 (lines 140-141) gives the second expert its own research, and row 3 (line 161) then claims 'their agreement means something'. These cannot both be in force. Under the amendment the two share the model's priors, the search ranking and the question list, so they will mostly find the same top papers and agree for the same reason. That is exactly risk 3, now presented as its cure. Disagreement no longer has a defined meaning either: it may come from different sources, not from a weak claim. No rule says what to do with either outcome.
findings.smallest_fix: Delete lines 79-80. Replace them with one scriptable rule: agreement between the two experts counts as independent support only when each side cites at least one confirmed card the other does not. Otherwise it is recorded as 'same evidence'. If the owner wants budget saved instead, drop second experts and spend that budget on the refuter of R3-03, since same-model sameness is the risk the ensemble was meant to cut.

findings.title: Nobody settles a disagreement of judgment; the adjudication can only settle disagreements of fact
findings.target: Section 6 'how results are combined', row 4, row 11, line 23
findings.argument: 'Facts are not voted on' and 'claims that conflict are both kept ... marked open; the coordinator may order one adjudication, in which a checker opens the cited sources again' (lines 83-86). Reopening sources settles a mis-transcribed number. Most expert conflicts are judgments, though: whether a result at 100k nodes transfers to our conditions, or whether a verdict is 'sound' or 'wrong form'. Both sides then cite confirmed cards, both claims 'stand', and nothing resolves them. They land on the owner's table (line 86), so the owner adjudicates expert disagreements himself, which is what the experts were for. Nothing says who detects a conflict. The synthesis is built 'by a script' (line 162), which cannot see that two prose claims conflict. Under row 11 the coordinator 'reads status files and verdicts only' (line 174), so it cannot choose which conflict to adjudicate. Experts never see each other's output (line 23), so neither side ever answers the other.
findings.smallest_fix: Give review.json one claim key per (approach id, measure), so the script lists every key where verdicts differ: that is the conflict detector. Send the conflicting rows, with both experts' cards, to the refuter of R3-03 (or to the methodologist for test-design conflicts). It writes one ruling per row in one round, and the ruling either names the decisive test or marks the row as open for a stated reason. This adds no new role.

findings.title: Our own files anchor the reviewer: the problem sheet is the coordinator's analysis of one repository, and our 'files without verdicts' contain verdicts
findings.target: Section 3 problem sheet, section 5 step 3, row 2, part C order of work
findings.argument: Line 65 says the expert 'is not given the coordinator's opinion'. Yet every expert gets the problem sheet, 'written by the coordinator from our own measurements' (lines 30-32), and the sheet ranks the sinks every lead is scored against. That is the coordinator's analysis, and it covers one repository. The direction's question is 'in general and not for one repository' (direction lines 11-13), and lane 1 explicitly includes 'published cost breakdowns of agents' (direction line 54), which the protocol drops. The 'results' given 'as files' (line 64) include reports that end in conclusions, for example the embeddings report saying no arm adds. Their file names (GRAPH-TEST-RESULT, the null in the report title), the order they are given in and the coordinator's choice of 'a fixed list per field' all frame the review. The question list itself comes from the direction file (line 36), whose section 2 is a list of hoped-for weaknesses. Row 2's 'neutral briefs' (line 160) has no one who checks neutrality. Part C (lines 187-188) says the other fields are 'judged by' the measurement field's criteria, but line 23 says experts never see each other's output, so that transfer has no channel.
findings.smallest_fix: Make the review two-pass. Pass one sees only the problem sheet and a neutral list of our assumptions (direction section 2 without its framing sentences), and it writes verdicts from cards and freezes them by hash. Pass two sees our results, and it may change a verdict only with a stated reason, which the script diffs. The problem sheet also takes in the measurement field's published breakdowns and criteria as a shared read-only input (allowed by line 90), with our sinks labelled 'one repository'.

findings.title: The review form forces a citation to exist, not the citation to support the sentence; the 'conclusion cards' check runs before conclusions exist
findings.argument: 'Every factual sentence cites a card ... anything else is marked as judgment' (lines 70-71). A schema can check that an id is present, not that the card says what the sentence claims. The commonest expert error is applying a card's result outside its conditions (repository size, model, task), and that passes. What counts as 'factual' is labelled by the expert itself. Row 1 says 'a checker reopens each card a conclusion rests on' (line 159). The checker runs in stage A (lines 44-45), and the conclusions are drawn in the stage B review, so at checking time nobody knows which cards conclusions will rest on. Cards that were only 'sampled' at gate A can carry the review's verdicts, and no step after the review reopens them.
findings.smallest_fix: Move the 'every card a conclusion rests on' check to after the review, and widen it slightly. The checker takes every card cited under a verdict, confirms it against its source, and judges whether the citing sentence stays within the card's conditions. The failure rate goes in the ledger, and a review above a set rate is returned once. This replaces the stage-A 'sample of the rest' rule; it does not add a role.

findings.title: Row 7's register of claimed sources stops an expert reading a paper central to its own field, and undoes the second expert's independence
findings.target: Row 7 against amendment 1 item 4 and the expert requirement
findings.argument: Row 7 keeps 'a shared register of claimed sources, one line per paper, checked by a helper before it reads' (line 170), to stop two fields reading the same source twice. The papers that matter most often sit in two fields: a graph-retrieval agent is lane 2, lane 4 and lane 7. Whichever field claims such a paper first, the other expert never reads it, so it is less of an expert to save a few thousand tokens. Within a field, a second expert who must 'do its own research' (lines 140-141) either cannot read the first expert's key papers, and so is not an expert, or it reads them, and then the register does nothing there. The row does not say which.
findings.smallest_fix: Remove the blocking. Keep the register as a read-only lookup: a field may reuse another field's confirmed card to save a reader's work, and it may always read the original. A field's pair of experts never share the register.

findings.title: The 300,000 ceiling will be the norm, not the exception, and the budget split no longer matches the design
findings.target: Amendment 1 item 5, row 12, section 4 step 4, section 9
findings.argument: A child under amendment 1 ingests the readers' cards and passages, then writes a pack of 60,000-90,000 tokens (lines 48-49), and that output stays in its window. The cards are therefore held twice, once as received and once as written into pack.md, before the five to eight must-read originals (line 50) and our files for review are added. 2 x 75k + 8 x 10-20k section reads + the review inputs is roughly 250-350k at the review, before tool overhead. Line 143's 'that is the exception' does not hold. The review, the most judgment-heavy step, therefore runs at the window's most crowded point, where long context hurts recall and weighing of evidence most. Row 12 (line 175) handles the cost of such windows, not their effect on judgment. Section 9 still splits the budget 'half for the packs, a quarter for the experts' (lines 121-122), roles amendment 1 merged into one session, so the split cannot be accounted. A window's size also understates its cost: every turn re-reads it, the measured sink row 11 itself names.
findings.smallest_fix: This is solved by R3-02's fix (review always in a fresh session at about 90k pack + must-read + our files), with no new rule. Then restate section 9 per field line as research session plus review session plus checks, with the figures set from the pilot field (row 14), not guessed.

findings.title: A 60,000-token floor on the pack pays for padding and works against 'nothing unnecessary'
findings.target: Section 4 step 4 and gate A size test
findings.argument: The pack 'stays within 60,000 to 90,000 tokens' (lines 48-49), and gate A fails a pack that does not 'fit the size' (line 54). A narrow or young field (lane 5 or lane 6 applied to coding harnesses) may have 20,000 tokens of real primary knowledge. To pass the gate the child must add marginal sources, so the floor buys exactly the 'unnecessary stuff' the owner ruled out (line 11; direction line 96). The ceiling has a purpose (window and cost); the floor has none.
findings.smallest_fix: Delete the lower bound: 'at most 90,000 tokens'. Coverage of the question list (line 53, as strengthened in R3-04) is the test of sufficiency, not word count.

findings.title: The B+ tree analogy changes no decision except one that harms expertise, and the tree-versus-single-session baseline has no score
findings.argument: 'Balanced' (line 181) restates section 2's three levels (lines 15-21). 'Inner nodes hold keys' (lines 182-183) restates row 11. The window half of 'split on overflow' restates amendment 1 item 5. The one new decision is splitting an outgrown field into two 'with question ranges that do not overlap' (lines 184-185), mid-run, against rule 1's fixed tree (line 90). That splits one expertise into two half-experts, and mechanisms that span the cut are reviewed by no one. The bullet that could actually test the owner's requirement, 'one field is also done by a single session without the tree, on the same budget' (lines 189-191), names no score. Without one, 'whether the tree earns its cost' can only be decided by impression after the fact.
findings.smallest_fix: Delete the first three bullets of part C. Replace field splitting with 'an outgrown field is narrowed by the owner, not split by the coordinator'. Give the baseline a score fixed in advance: the blind probe of R3-01 run on both arms, plus the R3-08 citation-support rate and the refuter's hit rate on each arm's review, together with tokens and time from the ledger.

rows_that_hold.row: Row 4 (hand-overs as files with fields; synthesis built by a script that cites cards)
rows_that_hold.why: A named mechanism with a runner (the schema script) and a stop (rejection on schema failure). Number, baseline and conditions travel as fields, so they cannot fall off a paraphrase. It fails only on conflicts of judgment (R3-06), which is not the risk it names.

rows_that_hold.row: Row 6 (one writer per folder, a branch per child, only the coordinator merges, schema check first)
rows_that_hold.why: Says who acts (the coordinator), when (before acceptance) and what stops the work (a failed schema check). The risk is fully covered.

rows_that_hold.row: Row 10 (state lives in the session's folder; restart from the folder)
rows_that_hold.why: Concrete and checkable: cards, pack and ledger lines are on disk, and a restart reads them. No session memory is load-bearing.

rows_that_hold.row: Row 11 (coordinator reads status only; hands over at 200,000 tokens)
rows_that_hold.why: A fixed threshold aimed at the measured main token sink, with a defined hand-over. It holds for its own risk. Its side effect on adjudication is R3-06, not a failure of the row.

rows_that_hold.row: Row 14 (a pilot field first, plan set from its measured tokens and time)
rows_that_hold.why: Turns the unknown cost into a measurement before scaling. It is also the right place to test R3-01's blind probe and R3-02's fresh reviewer.

rows_that_hold.row: Row 8 (three levels, helpers start nothing, six helpers per child, a total cap)
rows_that_hold.why: Numeric caps enforced by the structure itself: helpers have no ability to start agents.

rows_that_hold.row: Section 4 step 3 drop rule and the card schema (number, baseline, conditions, quote)
rows_that_hold.why: An unopenable or mismatched source is dropped by a named checker. That is a real mechanism against invented facts in the files (though not in a window that already read them, R3-02).

rows_that_hold.row: Section 5 step 4 fields 'cheapest decisive test' and 'what would change my mind'
rows_that_hold.why: They force every verdict to be falsifiable and to come with a test, which is the right form for a review the owner will choose experiments from.

rows_that_hold.row: Part C's single-session baseline on one field
rows_that_hold.why: The right control for whether the tree earns its cost. It needs only a score defined beforehand (R3-12).

result.overall: Read literally, the design does not yet deliver the owner's requirement, an expert first and a review that is not a raw opinion. Its anti-chaos machinery (rows 4, 6, 8, 10, 11 and 14) is sound. Its knowledge-and-judgment machinery is mostly wishes. Amendment 1 merged the researcher and the reviewer. That removed the one testable meaning of 'filled precisely' (a fresh window holding only the frozen pack) and makes the knowledge check a self-test: the child is graded against its own answer keys, so a session with wrong knowledge passes. Wrongly dropped cards stay in its head, and its review runs near a 300k window. Which sources get in is decided by search ranking and Sonnet screens, and no step checks selection, only transcription. The refuter is aimed at strong leads, while dismissed leads and dropped fields, the false negatives that started this programme, go unchallenged. A same-model second expert with the same search tool is not independent, and the comparison rule was written for the withdrawn design. Disagreements of judgment have no one to settle them, so they land on the owner. The problem sheet anchors every expert to one repository's sinks, against the direction's 'in general'. Most fixes remove or move rules rather than add machinery. The three that matter most: make the fresh-session review the rule, not the exception (needs the owner's word); write the probe blind, from sources rather than from the child's own cards; and aim the one refuter at dismissals. The pilot field is where to test all three before the tree is trusted.
